summary: This experimental RFC extends SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND), which protects IPv6 neighbor discovery with digital signatures. Plain SEND assumes the sender holds the keys for the address it speaks for, so a proxy that answers on another node's behalf cannot use it. The document defines how proxies can take part in SEND securely, mainly for mobility scenarios.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6496 extends SEND, the security scheme for IPv6 neighbour discovery, so that a router can answer on behalf of another node. The router is given a certificate saying which addresses it may speak for, and it signs its answers with its own key. A receiver checks that signature and the certificate before believing the answer.

subtitle: Letting a router answer neighbour discovery for another node, with a signature that proves it was allowed to.

tldr.problem: SEND signs neighbour discovery messages with the private key of the address owner or of the router, so a node that answers on another node's behalf cannot use it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo adds a Secure Proxy ND certificate that authorises a proxy for a range of addresses, a new Proxy Signature option that carries the proxy's signature, and processing rules that treat a message with a valid Proxy Signature option as secure.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document. It covers only the messages the proxy produces; the security of a proxied message without the new option is the same as for an unsecured message.

today: RFC 6496 is an Experimental document from February 2012, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends SEND with support for proxying Neighbor Discovery, and it depends on the companion document that defines the Secure Proxy ND certificate format.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SEND specifies a method for securing Neighbor Discovery signaling against specific threats. As defined today, SEND assumes that the node sending a Neighbor Discovery message is the owner of the address from which the message is sent, or possesses a key that authorizes the node to act as a router, so that it holds the private key or keys used to generate the digital signature on each message. This means the Proxy Neighbor Discovery signaling performed by nodes that do not hold the address owner's private key, or a router's key, cannot be secured using SEND.

The memo extends the SEND specification with support for Proxy Neighbor Discovery, and calls that extension Secure Proxy ND Support for SEND. The motivating problem is that a proxy advertises an address that is not its own, and under plain SEND the advertiser is required to generate a valid RSA Signature option, which in turn requires holding the key pair that was used to generate a Cryptographically Generated Address or that was associated to a router certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbour discovery in IPv6 lets a node ask who owns an address, and lets routers announce themselves. SEND signs those messages so nobody can lie. But the rule is that only the owner of an address, or an authorised router, may sign for it. A router that answers on behalf of a distant node therefore has nothing it is allowed to sign with.

sections.title: Secure Proxy ND Overview
sections.content:
The original SEND specification implicitly assumed that only the node sending a Neighbor Discovery message is the owner of the address it comes from. That assumption does not allow proxying, so the memo defines three extensions to separate the roles of owner and advertiser.

The first is a Secure Proxy ND certificate, a certificate authorizing an entity to act as a Neighbor Discovery proxy. It is an X.509v3 certificate in which the purpose for which the certificate is issued is specified explicitly, as described in a companion document. Such a certificate includes one or more KeyPurposeId values that can authorize a proxy to sign Router Advertisement and Redirect messages, or to sign Neighbor Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation or Router Solicitation messages on behalf of other nodes. The inclusion of this value allows the certificate owner to perform proxying of SEND messages for a range of addresses indicated in the same certificate, and the certificate can be exchanged through the Authorization Delegation Discovery process defined in SEND.

The second is a new Neighbor Discovery option called the Proxy Signature option. It contains the hash value of the public key of the proxy and the digital signature of the SEND message computed with the private key of the proxy. The hash is computed over the public key contained in the Secure Proxy ND certificate. When a Neighbor Discovery message contains a Proxy Signature option it must not contain CGA or RSA Signature options, and the Proxy Signature option must be appended to any Neighbor Discovery message to secure it.

The third is a modification of the SEND processing rules for all Neighbor Discovery messages: Neighbor Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation, Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement and Redirect. When any of these messages containing a Proxy Signature option is validated, it is considered secure.

The extensions are applied in a particular way. A Secure ND Proxy that proxies messages on behalf of a node uses the Proxy Signature option to protect them, and becomes part of the trusted infrastructure just like a SEND router. Messages built by synthesis follow the Neighbor Discovery for IPv6 specification, and translated messages result from the processing rules of the Neighbor Discovery Proxy specification. In order for nodes to validate secured proxied messages, the nodes must know the Secure Proxy ND certificate and apply the modified processing rules; the memo calls these SPND nodes. The rules for generating messages in SPND nodes do not change, so those nodes behave as defined in SEND when they send messages. To let SPND nodes know the certification path required to validate the public key of the proxy, devices responding to Certification Path Solicitation messages with Certification Path Advertisement messages are extended to support the certificate format, and are configured with the appropriate certification path.
sections.plainLanguage: Three pieces work together. A certificate says which addresses a proxy may speak for. A new option in the message carries the proxy's signature. And the checking rules on the receiving side treat a message with that option as genuine. A proxy that has this certificate becomes as trusted as a router.

sections.title: The Proxy Signature Option
sections.content:
The Proxy Signature option allows signatures based on public keys to be attached to Neighbor Discovery messages. Its layout has a Type field whose value is 32, a Length field giving the length of the option including the Type, Length, Reserved, Key Hash, Digital Signature and Padding fields in units of 8 octets, a 16-bit Reserved field that the sender must initialize to zero and the receiver must ignore, a 128-bit Key Hash field, a variable-length Digital Signature field, and a variable-length Padding field.

The Key Hash holds the most significant, leftmost, 128 bits of a SHA-1 hash of the public key used for constructing the signature. Its purpose is to associate the signature with a particular key known by the receiver, and such a key must be the same one within the corresponding Secure Proxy ND certificate.

The Digital Signature is a variable-length field containing a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature, constructed with the sender's private key over a sequence of octets. The sequence is: the 128-bit CGA Message Type tag value for Secure Proxy ND, which is 0x09F5 2BE5 3B62 4C76 CB96 4E7F CDC9 2804 and was generated randomly by the editor of the specification; the 128-bit Source Address field from the IP header; the 128-bit Destination Address field from the IP header; the 8-bit Type, 8-bit Code and 16-bit Checksum fields from the ICMP header; the NDP message header, starting from the octet after the ICMP Checksum field and continuing up to but not including NDP options; and all the NDP options preceding the Proxy Signature option. The signature is computed with the RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 algorithm and a SHA-1 hash, and its length is determined by the ASN.1 BER coding of the PKCS#1 v1.5 signature. The Padding field holds the padding, and its length is the length of the option minus the length of the other fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The option carries a fingerprint of the proxy's public key, so the receiver knows which key to check against, and a signature over the parts of the packet that matter: the addresses, the ICMP header, the message header and the options that came before it. The proxy's own option is left out of the signed part.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
A Secure ND Proxy performs all the operations described in the SEND specification, with new processing rules so that the receiving node can identify an authorized proxy generating a translated or synthetic message for a proxied address. The signature of the proxy is performed over all the Neighbor Discovery Protocol options present in the message, and the Proxy Signature option is appended as the last option.

On the sending side, a proxy must not use a key to sign message types that do not correspond to the authorization granted to that key. Neighbor Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation and Router Solicitation messages must be signed with a key whose certificate carries a KeyPurposeId of id-kp-sendProxiedOwner, and the source addresses of the messages must be encompassed in the prefix associated with that certificate. Router Advertisement and Redirect messages must be signed with a key whose certificate carries a KeyPurposeId of id-kp-sendProxiedRouter, and the prefix included in the Router Advertisement for on-link determination or stateless address autoconfiguration, and the Target Address of the Redirect, must be encompassed in that prefix. A secured message sent by a proxy for a proxied address must contain a Proxy Signature option and must not contain either CGA or RSA Signature options.

The input to the process is either a synthetic message, which must be constructed as described in the Neighbor Discovery for IPv6 specification, or a translated message. For translation, the authenticity of the intercepted message must first be verified: if it is a SEND message it must be validated as specified in SEND, and if it contains a Proxy Signature option its authenticity must be verified under the receiver rules. After validation the CGA, RSA or Proxy Signature options of the original message must be removed, and the message to be translated is processed according to the Neighbor Discovery Proxy specification. The proxy then adds Timestamp and Nonce options according to the rules in SEND, with the timestamp generated by the proxy and the nonce taken from the intercepted message when translating one, generated by the proxy when synthesising a solicitation, and corresponding to the solicitation being answered when synthesising an advertisement. Finally the Proxy Signature option is added as the last option and the data is signed.

On the receiving side, a SEND message without a Proxy Signature option is treated as specified in SEND. A message with one is processed as follows. The receiver must ignore any RSA and CGA options and any options that come after the first Proxy Signature option, for both signature verification and Neighbor Discovery processing. The Key Hash must indicate a known public key, with a valid certification path known between the receiver's trust anchor and the sender's public key, and the certificate must contain the appropriate KeyPurposeId value and prefix for the message, so id-kp-sendProxiedRouter for Router Advertisement and Redirect messages and id-kp-sendProxiedOwner for Neighbor Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation and Router Solicitation messages. The Digital Signature field must have correct encoding and its verification must show that the signature was calculated as specified. The Nonce and Timestamp options are then processed as in SEND with the RSA Signature option replaced by the Proxy Signature option, and the receiver should store the peer-related timing information separately for each different proxy, identified by the different Key Hash values, and separately from the timing information for the address being proxied. Messages with the Override bit set must override an existing cache entry regardless of how it was created, and when the Override bit is not set the advertisement must not update a cached link-layer address created securely. Messages whose verification fails must be silently discarded if the node accepts only secured messages, and may be accepted but treated as unsecured otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: The proxy signs with a key that its certificate allows for that kind of message and that address range. The receiver ignores anything after the proxy's option, checks that the certificate matches the message, checks the signature, and applies the usual freshness checks. A message that fails is either thrown away or treated as unsigned, depending on the node's configuration.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The memo discusses how a Secure ND Proxy behaves when the nodes it serves do not all implement the same things. A node that does not implement SEND at all is called a non-SEND node, and one that implements SEND as defined in RFC 3971 but not this specification is called an RFC 3971 node. A node that receives and validates messages according to this specification is a Secure Proxy ND node.

The rule the memo gives is that a Secure ND Proxy must synthesize and translate messages containing the Proxy Signature option for SPND and RFC 3971 hosts, and must not do so for non-SEND nodes. Neighbor Discovery advertisements in response to solicitations generated by a Secure ND Proxy must either be secured or not secured according to the nature of the proxied node, not according to the secure or unsecured nature of the solicitation message.

To apply this rule, the proxy needs to know the security capabilities of the proxied node, and how that information is acquired depends on the scenario. For scenarios in which messages are translated for nodes that can arrive on the link where the proxy operates, only messages validated under SEND, or under the receiver rules of this memo for messages containing a Proxy Signature option, must be proxied securely. Unsecured messages could be proxied if unsecured operation is enabled, but the message the proxy produces must not include a Proxy Signature option.

For scenarios in which messages are synthesized on behalf of remote nodes, the considerations differ. For Mobile IPv6, if the mobile node can return to the home link, the proxy has to know whether the node could use SEND to defend its address. A home agent that included the Proxy Signature option for a non-SEND mobile node would make the messages it sends more preferred than the messages of that node when it returns, and not using the option for an RFC 3971 or SPND mobile node would make the address in the home link more vulnerable while the node was away, defeating the purpose of the mechanism. The memo also notes that a configuration option may exist in a proxy to specify the non-SEND nodes it is connected to, so that the messages sent to them are not processed under this specification, for performance reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks mix nodes that understand SEND, nodes that understand only the original SEND, and nodes that understand neither. The proxy has to decide when to use the new option, and the rule follows the node being served rather than the message it received.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism introduces a new option allowing a proxy to synthesize or translate a message for a proxied address, to redirect traffic for given target addresses, or to advertise prefix information by means of Router Advertisement messages. An SPND node accepts such a message only if it includes a valid Proxy Signature option generated by a properly authorized proxy, with a certificate carrying a KeyPurposeId of id-kp-sendProxiedOwner for the Neighbor Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation and Router Solicitation messages, or id-kp-sendProxiedRouter for the Router Advertisement and Redirect messages. Such a message has protection against the threats presented in SEND equivalent to a message signed with an RSA Signature option.

The security of proxied messages that do not include a Proxy Signature option is the same as that of an unsecured message, and so is the security of a proxied message received by a non-SEND host or an RFC 3971 host. When a message including a Proxy Signature option is received by an SPND node, any CGA or RSA options also included are removed and the remaining message processed. Although properly formed proxied messages must not include Proxy Signature and CGA or RSA options at the same time, discarding them if they appear does not affect security. If the option validates, the information in the message was validly generated by a proxy and should be honored, with anti-replay protection provided by the Nonce and Timestamp options. If it does not validate, the message is treated as unsecured. There is no gain for an attacker from appending false or old CGA or RSA information to a message secured by a proxy.

The memo notes that a compromised proxy holding a certificate with id-kp-sendProxiedRouter can, like a compromised router, siphon off traffic from the host or mount a man-in-the-middle attack for hosts communicating to off-link hosts. A compromised proxy holding id-kp-sendProxiedOwner can do the same for communication between on-link hosts, even if those hosts use SEND.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed proxy message is as trustworthy as one signed by a router. But a proxy that has been compromised is a serious problem: it can reroute traffic for the addresses it is trusted to speak for, which is the same risk a compromised router carries.

viz.caption: THE THREE EXTENSIONS THAT SECURE PROXY ND ADDS

items.title: Secure Proxy ND certificate
items.text: An X.509v3 certificate that authorizes an entity to act as a proxy, with a KeyPurposeId for the messages it may sign.

items.title: Proxy Signature option
items.text: A new Neighbor Discovery option carrying a hash of the proxy's public key and the proxy's signature over the message.

items.title: Modified SEND processing rules
items.text: A Neighbor Discovery message that carries a valid Proxy Signature option is treated as secure.

fields.desc: The option type, whose value is 32.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the option in units of 8 octets, including the signature and padding.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved for future use; the sender must set it to zero and the receiver must ignore it.

fields.name: Key Hash
fields.desc: The leftmost 128 bits of a SHA-1 hash of the public key used to construct the signature, so the receiver knows which key to check.
